title: Options from zero: rights, obligations, and the four basic positions

reading.h: Two contracts, two verbs: call up, put down
reading.body:
Every provider says the same thing: **more people fail the Series 7 because of options than any other topic.** So this module starts them at the SIE stage and never lets go. The good news is that all of it is built from four simple positions — get those four cold and spreads, straddles and hedges become bookkeeping on top of them.

An option is a contract on **100 shares** of an underlying stock. There are only two kinds.

A **call** is the right to *buy* the stock at a fixed price. You want a call when you think the stock will go **up** — you can buy it cheap and it is worth more.

A **put** is the right to *sell* the stock at a fixed price. You want a put when you think the stock will go **down** — you can sell high while the market is low.

The memory hook is **"call up, put down"**: call it up, put it down. The fixed price is the **strike** (or exercise) price; the last day the contract is alive is **expiration**.

reading.h: Rights vs. obligations — who pays whom
reading.body:
This is the hinge the whole topic turns on. Every contract has two sides.

The **buyer** (also called the *holder* or the *long*) pays a **premium** and gets a **right** — they may exercise or may walk away. Because they can always walk away, a buyer's loss is capped at the premium paid.

The **writer** (the *seller*, the *short*) collects the premium and takes on an **obligation** — if the buyer exercises, the writer must perform. The premium is the writer's to keep no matter what; in exchange they carry the risk.

Model it as **insurance**: the buyer is the policyholder paying a premium for protection; the writer is the insurance company collecting premiums and hoping never to pay a claim. Buyers have limited risk; writers accept the larger risk.

reading.h: The premium and the times-100 multiplier
reading.body:
Premiums are quoted **per share**, but one contract covers **100 shares**. So the dollar cost is always **premium × 100**.

"ABC Jan 50 call @ 3" means: a call on ABC, strike $50, expiring in January, premium $3 per share. One contract costs **3 × 100 = $300**.

Forgetting the ×100 is the single most common arithmetic slip on the whole exam. A "$3" answer choice will always be sitting there to catch people who quote the per-share number. Whenever you see a premium, immediately think in hundreds of dollars.

reading.h: Moneyness: intrinsic value, and why premium is ignored
reading.body:
**Intrinsic value** is how much an option is *in the money* right now — the real, exercise-today value. It is never negative.

For a **call**, intrinsic value = stock price − strike (when the stock is above the strike). For a **put**, intrinsic value = strike − stock price (when the stock is below the strike).

Example: ABC trades at 58. An ABC 50 **call** has intrinsic value 58 − 50 = **8** (in the money). An ABC 50 **put** has intrinsic value 0 (out of the money — you would not sell at 50 when the market pays 58).

Two rules the exam loves: **moneyness ignores the premium** (you classify by stock vs. strike only), and **it is the same for the buyer and the writer**. A call is in the money when the stock is above the strike — whether you are long it or short it. "A short call is in the money when the stock is above the strike" is TRUE.

Every options question is built from these four. Learn the row, not the cell.

**Long call** — bullish. Max gain **unlimited** (stock can keep rising); max loss the **premium**; breakeven = **strike + premium**.

**Short (naked) call** — bearish/neutral. Max gain the **premium**; max loss **UNLIMITED** (the writer must deliver stock at any price); breakeven = **strike + premium**.

**Long put** — bearish. Max gain = **strike − premium** (best case: stock goes to zero); max loss the **premium**; breakeven = **strike − premium**.

**Short (naked) put** — bullish/neutral. Max gain the **premium**; max loss = **strike − premium**; breakeven = **strike − premium**.

Three things to burn in: **calls add** the premium to the strike, **puts subtract** it; **the buyer and the writer of the same contract share the same breakeven**; and the only single position with truly **unlimited** loss is the **short call** (because only a stock price has no ceiling).

**Long 1 ABC Jun 50 call @ 4.** Breakeven = 50 + 4 = **54**. Max loss = the $400 premium. If ABC is 60 at expiration: intrinsic 10, minus the 4 paid = +6 × 100 = **+$600**. If ABC is 45: the call expires worthless, loss **−$400**.

**Long 1 XYZ Sep 40 put @ 3.** Breakeven = 40 − 3 = **37**. Max loss = the $300 premium. Best case, XYZ falls to 0: gain (40 − 3) × 100 = **+$3,700**. If XYZ is 30 at expiration: intrinsic 10, minus 3 = +7 × 100 = **+$700**.

Notice the writer of that same put has breakeven 37 too — the shared-breakeven rule in action.

reading.h: Who stands behind the contract: the OCC and the ODD
reading.body:
Listed options are standardized and guaranteed by the **Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)**. The OCC is the *issuer and guarantor* of every listed option: it sets the standard terms (100-share size, strike intervals, expiration dates), clears every trade, and assigns exercises. Because the OCC stands between every buyer and every writer, a holder never has to worry about a particular writer's credit.

Before a customer's first options trade, they must receive the OCC's **Options Disclosure Document (ODD)** — the booklet "Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options."

One more distinction you will see: **American-style** options can be exercised any business day up to expiration (all equity options); **European-style** options can be exercised only *at* expiration (most index options). Style limits *exercise*, not *trading* — both trade freely until they expire.

flashcards.front: Call vs. put in one phrase
flashcards.back: Call = right to BUY (bullish, "call up"). Put = right to SELL (bearish, "put down").

flashcards.front: Buyer vs. writer: rights and money
flashcards.back: Buyer pays the premium and holds a RIGHT (limited loss). Writer collects the premium and takes an OBLIGATION (larger risk).
Premium × 100. "@ 3" = $300 per contract. Forgetting ×100 is the most common exam error.

flashcards.front: Intrinsic value of a call / of a put
flashcards.back: Call: stock − strike. Put: strike − stock. Never negative; premium is ignored.

flashcards.front: Is moneyness different for the writer?
flashcards.back: No. Moneyness compares stock to strike and is identical for buyer and writer. A short call is ITM when stock > strike.

flashcards.front: Long call: outlook, max gain, max loss, breakeven
flashcards.back: Bullish; unlimited gain; loss = premium; BE = strike + premium.
UNLIMITED — the only single position with no ceiling (stock can rise forever). BE = strike + premium.

flashcards.front: Long put: max gain and breakeven
flashcards.back: Max gain = strike − premium (stock to zero); BE = strike − premium.

flashcards.front: Short put: max loss and breakeven
flashcards.back: Max loss = strike − premium; BE = strike − premium; max gain = the premium.
Puts subtract. Call BE = strike + premium; put BE = strike − premium. Buyer and writer share the same breakeven.
Options Clearing Corporation — issuer and guarantor of every listed option; standardizes terms, clears trades, assigns exercises.
American = exercise any business day (equity options). European = exercise only at expiration (most index options). Both trade freely until expiry.

quiz.stem: An investor pays $200 for a contract giving her the right, but not the obligation, to buy 100 shares of ABC at $50. ABC then falls to $40. What is her best course of action and her result?
options: Exercise and buy the shares at $50, losing $1,000
Let the contract expire unused, losing only the $200 premium
Demand a refund of the $200 because the stock moved against her
Buy the shares at $40 and pay a $200 penalty
quiz.explanation: A call buyer holds a RIGHT, not a duty. Buying at $50 when the market is $40 makes no sense, so she walks away and the call expires; her loss is capped at the $200 premium. There is no refund — the premium was the price of the right, and it belongs to the writer.

quiz.stem: A customer expects XYZ to DECLINE over the next two months and wants a position with limited risk. Which is MOST appropriate?
options: Long XYZ call
Short XYZ call
Long XYZ put
Short XYZ put
quiz.explanation: A long put is bearish ("put down") with loss limited to the premium. A short call is also bearish but carries UNLIMITED risk, so it fails the limited-risk requirement. A long call and a short put are both bullish.

quiz.stem: An option is quoted at 2.50 per share and an investor buys one contract. What is the MOST this buyer can lose?
options: Unlimited, because the stock could keep moving against him
quiz.explanation: Premiums are per share and a contract covers 100 shares: 2.50 × 100 = $250. A buyer can never lose more than the premium. "$2.50" forgets the ×100 multiplier; "unlimited" applies to a naked writer, not a buyer.

quiz.stem: ABC stock trades at 56. An ABC Oct 50 call is in the money for:
options: both the holder and the writer
the holder only; the writer is out of the money
the writer only, because the writer collected the premium
neither party until the stock exceeds 50 plus the premium
quiz.explanation: Moneyness compares stock to strike (56 − 50 = 6 in the money), ignores the premium, and is identical for both sides. A call is ITM whenever the stock is above the strike, whether you are long or short it.

quiz.stem: Which BEST describes the role of the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)?
options: It issues and guarantees every listed option and standardizes the contract terms
It sets the premium at which each contract trades
It approves each customer's options account before the first trade
It publishes buy and sell recommendations for options traders
quiz.explanation: The OCC is the issuer and guarantor of all listed options; it standardizes terms, clears trades, and assigns exercises. Premiums are set by the market, and an account is approved by a Registered Options Principal — not by the OCC.

quiz.stem: A customer buys 1 DEF Mar 30 call at 2. What is the breakeven point at expiration?
quiz.explanation: Calls ADD: breakeven = strike + premium = 30 + 2 = 32, the same for buyer and writer. "28" applies the put rule (subtract), "30" forgets the premium, and "34" double-counts it.

quiz.stem: Maria writes a put and collects a $300 premium from Dan. At expiration the put is out of the money and Dan lets it expire. What happens to the $300?
options: It is refunded to Dan because he never exercised
It is split evenly between the two parties
The exchange holds it until a new contract is written
Maria keeps it; the premium is hers whether or not the option is exercised
quiz.explanation: The premium is paid to the writer up front as the price of the right and is never refunded. If the option expires unused, the writer's gain is the entire premium — here, Maria's $300.
